paper.title: Reconstruction from Milnor K-theory, modulo the characteristic
paper.html:
Abstract

Let K and L be finitely generated extensions of transcendence degree at least two over algebraically closed fields of characteristic p. We prove that every isomorphism of their first Milnor K-groups modulo p preserving the degree-two Steinberg relations is a nonzero scalar multiple of the map induced by a unique field isomorphism. The proof recovers projective lines over the subfields of pth powers by an elementary calculation with derivations.

1 Introduction

Milnor K-theory records multiplication in a field together with relations arising from addition. A reconstruction problem asks whether this information determines the field, and whether isomorphisms of the invariant come from field isomorphisms. We study this question in characteristic p using only the first two Milnor K-groups modulo p.
Fix a prime p and write Λ=Fp​. For a field F of characteristic p, set
VF​=F×/(F×)p=K1M​(F)/p.
We write [f] for the class of f∈F× and use additive notation in VF​: thus [f]+[g]=[fg], r[f]=[fr] for r∈Z, and [1]=0. Define the Steinberg relation subspace
RF​=SpanΛ​{[f]⊗[1−f]:f∈F∖{0,1}}⊂VF​⊗Λ​VF​.
The quotient WF​=(VF​⊗Λ​VF​)/RF​ is K2M​(F)/p by the tensor presentation of Milnor K-theory [Milnor, 1970, Section~1]. We denote the image of [f]⊗[g] in WF​ by {f,g}F​.
Let IsomM​(VK​,VL​) be the set of Λ-linear isomorphisms Θ:VK​→VL​ satisfying
(Θ⊗Θ)(RK​)=RL​.
We call these isomorphisms compatible. Equivalently, Θ extends to an isomorphism of the degree-one and degree-two groups respecting their product pairing. Scalar multiplication by Λ× acts on this set. For specified subfields k⊂K and l⊂L, write Isom(K,k;L,l) for the field isomorphisms α:K→L with α(k)=l. Such an isomorphism induces α∗​([f])=[α(f)] and carries RK​ onto RL​.
Theorem 1.1.
Let K/k and L/l be finitely generated extensions of algebraically closed fields of characteristic p, with
trdeg(K/k)≥2,trdeg(L/l)≥2.
The canonical map
Isom(K,k;L,l)⟶IsomM​(VK​,VL​)/Λ×,α⟼[α∗​],
is bijective.
The invariant therefore determines the field and its isomorphisms, with exactly the scalar identification in the displayed target. The argument also recovers the named algebraically closed base from the field itself.

1.1 Context and method

Bogomolov and Tschinkel developed a reconstruction method that recovers projective lines from multiplication and algebraic dependence, and applied it to Milnor K-theory in characteristic zero [Bogomolov and Tschinkel, 2009]. Cadoret and Pirutka extended reconstruction from the multiplicative group modulo constants and algebraic dependence to finitely generated regular extensions of perfect fields [Cadoret and Pirutka, 2021, Theorem~4]. For algebraically closed or finite base fields, they also obtained reconstruction from suitable quotients of the Milnor K-ring [Cadoret and Pirutka, 2021, Corollary~10].
Reconstruction from other reduced forms of K-theory has also been studied. For a prime ℓ different from the characteristic, Topaz recovers perfect closures from mod-ℓ data together with rational subgroups for function fields over algebraically closed bases in transcendence degree at least five [Topaz, 2016, Theorem~B]. His work on rational Milnor K-theory reconstructs perfect closures for fields of absolute transcendence degree at least five [Topaz, 2023, Main Theorem]. Theorem 1.1 concerns reduction modulo the characteristic and starts directly from VF​ and RF​; neither rational subgroups nor algebraic-dependence data are supplied.
The geometric framework of our proof has close predecessors. A differential approach to line recovery appears in an argument of Rovinsky recorded by Bogomolov and Tschinkel [Bogomolov and Tschinkel, 2012, Proposition~9]. In positive characteristic, Cadoret and Pirutka recover projective lines over the subfield of pth powers after a common power correction, using a differential intersection calculation [Cadoret and Pirutka, 2021, Section~1.3, Lemma~23, and Proposition~27]. Here the intersection calculation involves only degree-p extensions of the subfield of pth powers. The resulting intersection statement, Proposition 3.1, and the passage from vanishing symbols to these subextensions are given complete elementary proofs below. These are the two structural ingredients that allow the degree-two mod-p relations to supply the required projective geometry.

1.2 Outline of the proof

Put CF​=Fp. Since (F×)p=CF×​, the underlying set of VF​ is the projective point set PCF​​(F). Its point [1] is the zero of the group VF​; its projective lines are the sets of one-dimensional subspaces in two-dimensional CF​-subspaces of F. The field degree is finite:
[F:CF​]=ptrdeg(F/κ)
for F/κ as in the theorem. This is a projective geometry over CF​, not over the original constant field κ.
The first step constrains pairs with vanishing symbol. If s∈/CF​ and {s,t}F​=0, then t∈CF​(s). To prove this implication, consider a p-independent pair s,t, meaning that [CF​(s,t):CF​]=p2. Extend it to a monomial basis and take the determinant of two logarithmic derivatives. This pairing kills Steinberg relations and is nonzero on the independent pair. Section 2 supplies the details.
The fields CF​(s) need not themselves be two-dimensional over CF​, so this implication does not yet recover projective lines. The key calculation in Section 3 uses intersections of two multiplicative translates of such subfields. For a p-independent pair X,Y, suppose U∈CF​(X)× and V∈CF​(Y)× are not scalar multiples of powers of X,Y, respectively. A nonzero element of
XCF​(Y/X) ∩ UCF​(V/U)
forces, for a unique 1≤n<p,
Un∈CF​+CF​Xn,Vn∈CF​+CF​Yn.
Euler derivations give this common exponent and show that either inclusion determines it.
Section 4 produces the required intersections from Steinberg relations. Uniqueness propagates the exponent across a connected graph, giving one scalar n for which nΘ preserves every projective line. Applying the argument to the inverse, and using the fact that no nontrivial scalar preserves projective lines, yields preservation in both directions. Section 5 then proves the needed projective lifting theorem and uses the multiplicative group law to turn the normalized semilinear lift into a field isomorphism. Finally, the identity ⋂m≥1​Fpm=κ recovers the original base and completes the theorem.

2 Symbols and projective points over pth powers

Let F/κ be a finitely generated extension of an algebraically closed field of characteristic p, and put
C=Fp,d=trdeg(F/κ).
Since (F×)p=C×, the underlying set of VF​ is the point set of the projective space PC​(F): the class [f] represents the one-dimensional C-subspace Cf. These projective points also carry the Fp​-vector-space structure [f]+[g]=[fg], whose zero is [1]. We will use both structures, keeping their two scalar fields distinct. Our first task is to extract from a vanishing symbol the field-theoretic constraint that will allow us to recover projective lines.
Lemma 2.1.
With the notation above, [F:C]=pd.
Proof.
Choose a transcendence basis t1​,…,td​ over κ, and write F0​=κ(t1​,…,td​). Perfectness of κ gives F0p​=κ(t1p​,…,tdp​). The monomials t1i1​​⋯tdid​​ with 0≤ij​<p form a basis of F0​ over F0p​: group polynomial exponents modulo p, and for rational functions use a/b=abp−1/bp. Linear independence follows by clearing denominators and separating the exponent classes. Thus [F0​:F0p​]=pd.
The extension F/F0​ is finite, and Frobenius induces an isomorphism of extensions F/F0​≃Fp/F0p​. Computing [F:F0p​] in the two towers through F0​ and Fp gives
[F:F0​]pd=[F:Fp][Fp:F0p​]=[F:Fp][F:F0​].
Cancellation proves the assertion without a separability assumption.
∎
A list s1​,…,sr​∈F is p-independent over C if [C(s1​,…,sr​):C]=pr. A p-independent list generating F over C is called a p-basis. Its monomials supply derivations that record one exponent at a time.
Lemma 2.2.
Let F be any field of characteristic p, and put C=Fp. If C⊆M⊆F and s∈F∖M, then [M(s):M]=p. If [F:C] is finite, every p-independent list extends to a p-basis s1​,…,se​ of F/C, with [F:C]=pe and monomial basis
{s1i1​​⋯seie​​:0≤ij​<p}.
For such a basis there are commuting C-linear derivations D1​,…,De​ on F satisfying
Dj​(s1i1​​⋯seie​​)=ij​s1i1​​⋯seie​​.
On C(sj​) the kernel of Dj​ is C, and its nonzero eigenvectors with eigenvalue in C are precisely the elements csji​, where c∈C× and 0≤i<p; their eigenvalues are i∈Fp​. Moreover, C(sj​)∩C(sk​)=C when j=k.
Proof.
Since sp∈C, the minimal polynomial of s over M divides Tp−sp=(T−s)p. If its degree were 1≤e<p, it would be (T−s)e, and its coefficient −es of Te−1 would force s∈M. Thus every strict adjunction has degree p. When [F:C] is finite, successive adjunctions must terminate, so they extend any p-independent list to a generating list. If its length is e, the tower formula gives [F:C]=pe, and the usual basis of each simple extension gives the asserted monomial basis.
Define the Dj​ on these monomials and extend C-linearly. When two monomials are multiplied, reducing an exponent by p only removes a factor in C and leaves its value in Fp​ unchanged. This proves the product rule. The operators commute because they are diagonal on the same basis. On C(sj​) their eigenvector assertions follow from the distinct eigenvalues 0,1,…,p−1 on 1,sj​,…,sjp−1​. Finally, the expansions of an element in both C(sj​) and C(sk​) can have only their constant term in common.
∎
For a p-independent pair s,t, write Ds​,Dt​ for the corresponding derivations obtained from any extending p-basis. The following proof uses a coordinate form of the logarithmic differential symbol; the much stronger injectivity theorem for that symbol is the Bloch–Gabber–Kato theorem [Bloch and Kato, 1986, Theorem~(2.1)]. Here we check the needed implication directly.
Lemma 2.3.
For s,t∈F×, one has
s∈/C,{s,t}F​=0⟹t∈C(s).
Proof.
Suppose instead that s∈/C and t∈/C(s). By Lemma 2.2, the pair s,t is p-independent. Consider
β([f],[g])=fDs​f​gDt​g​−fDt​f​gDs​g​,f,g∈F×.
Each logarithmic derivative is additive on products and vanishes on C×. Hence β is a well-defined Fp​-bilinear map VF​×VF​→F. For f=0,1, the identities Ds​(1−f)=−Ds​f and Dt​(1−f)=−Dt​f give β([f],[1−f])=0. Thus β descends through the Steinberg relations to an Fp​-linear map WF​→F. But Ds​s=s, Dt​t=t, and Ds​t=Dt​s=0, so this map sends {s,t}F​ to 1. The symbol cannot vanish.
∎
The symbols arising from an affine line do vanish, by the defining Steinberg relation itself.
Lemma 2.4.
If c,d∈C× and t,c+dt∈F×, then
{t,c+dt}F​=0.
Proof.
Put q=−dt/c. The hypotheses give q=0,1, while [q]=[t] and [1−q]=[c+dt], since the omitted factors lie in C×. Therefore the identity is the Steinberg relation {q,1−q}F​=0.
∎

3 An intersection that determines an exponent

For X∈F∖C, the projective line through [1] and [X] consists of the nonzero elements of C+CX, modulo C×. To recover such lines from degree-p subfields, we need to pass from membership in C(X) to membership in C+CX, possibly after taking a power. The following intersection provides such a condition for two p-independent elements at once. Its uniqueness assertion will allow the exponent to be compared between different pairs.
The use of differential equations to control such intersections, including the power correction in positive characteristic, appears in Cadoret and Pirutka (2021), Sections~3.4--3.5. Here the degree-p subextensions allow a direct proof using commuting Euler derivations.
Proposition 3.1 (Intersection and exponent).
Let F be a field of characteristic p with [F:Fp]<∞, and put C=Fp. Let X,Y∈F× be p-independent. Suppose
U∈C(X)×,V∈C(Y)×,[U]∈/Fp​[X],[V]∈/Fp​[Y].
If
XC(Y/X)× ∩ UC(V/U)×=∅,(3.1)
then there is a unique integer n, 1≤n<p, such that
Un∈C+CXn,Vn∈C+CYn.(3.2)
In fact, either inclusion in (3.2) determines n uniquely. In each inclusion, both coefficients are nonzero.
The shape of (3.1) reflects the inclusion CX+CY⊆XC(Y/X), and its counterpart for U,V. Thus a common nonzero vector of the two spans yields the required intersection.
Proof.
Choose Z in the intersection (3.1). Extend X,Y to a p-basis and let DX​,DY​ be the commuting Euler derivations of Lemma 2.2. We first translate the two descriptions of Z into differential equations. Since U and V are not scalar multiples of monomials in X and Y, respectively, the eigenvector description in that lemma gives
DX​U=0,DY​V=0.
Define
BX​=DX​UU​,BY​=DY​VV​,AX​=BX​−1,AY​=BY​−1.
Here AX​∈C(X)∖C and AY​∈C(Y)∖C: if, for example, BX​∈C, then DX​U=BX−1​U, making U an eigenvector and hence a scalar multiple of a monomial in X. In particular, AX​,AY​,BX​,BY​ are all nonzero.
The derivations
δ=DX​+DY​,δ′=BX​DX​+BY​DY​
satisfy δX=X, δY=Y, δ′U=U, and δ′V=V. Thus δ kills Y/X, whereas δ′ kills V/U; both kill C. The two expressions for Z therefore give
δZ=Z=δ′Z.
Set
qX​=ZDX​Z​,qY​=ZDY​Z​.
Dividing the preceding equations by Z and subtracting yields
qX​+qY​=1,AX​qX​+AY​qY​=0.(3.3)
Both qX​ and qY​ are nonzero: if one vanished, these two equations would force the other A to vanish.
Since δ commutes with DX​ and DY​, the equation δZ=Z implies that qX​,qY​ are killed by δ:
δqX​=ZDX​(δZ)​−Z2DX​ZδZ​=0,δqY​=0.
By (3.3), AX​/AY​=−qY​/qX​, so δ(AX​/AY​)=0. Since DY​AX​=DX​AY​=0, we obtain
AX​DX​AX​​=AY​DY​AY​​.(3.4)
The left side lies in C(X) and the right side in C(Y). Their intersection is C, by the p-monomial basis. Consequently AX​ and AY​ are eigenvectors of their respective Euler derivations with the same eigenvalue. The distinct eigenvalues on 1,X,…,Xp−1, and on 1,Y,…,Yp−1, now give
AX​=cX​Xm,AY​=cY​Ym(3.5)
for cX​,cY​∈C× and one integer m, 1≤m<p. The eigenvalue cannot be zero because AX​,AY​∈/C.
It remains to integrate (3.5) inside the one-variable subfields. Put n=p−m. The identity 1+cX​Xm=BX​=0 ensures that all terms in
UnDX​(Un)​=1+cX​Xmn​=Xn+cX​XpDX​(Xn+cX​Xp)​
are defined. Thus DX​ kills Un/(Xn+cX​Xp)∈C(X)×. Its kernel on C(X) is C, so this quotient belongs to C×. Since Xp∈C×, we have Un∈C+CXn with both coefficients nonzero. Replacing X,U,cX​,DX​ by Y,V,cY​,DY​ proves the second inclusion.
Finally, suppose Ur=h+jXr with h,j∈C and 1≤r<p. Both coefficients must be nonzero: otherwise r[U]∈Fp​[X], contrary to [U]∈/Fp​[X]. Taking logarithmic derivatives gives
UDX​U​=h+jXrjXr​,AX​=jXrh​.
The last expression is a nonzero scalar multiple of Xp−r, since Xp∈C×. Comparison with (3.5) and linear independence of the p monomials forces p−r=m, hence r=n. The argument for the inclusion involving V is identical.
∎
All hypotheses and conclusions of Proposition 3.1 are unchanged when X,Y,U,V are multiplied by elements of C×. In particular, its exponent depends on projective points, rather than on the representatives used in the calculation.

4 One scalar recovers all projective lines

The intersection calculation produces a power correction for two points at a time. We now show that a single correction works throughout the projective space. The passage from local power corrections to a global one parallels Cadoret and Pirutka (2021), Section~3.5; here the degree-p subfields give a particularly simple connected graph on which to propagate the correction.
We first record why a nontrivial scalar cannot preserve projective lines. This will rule out a new scalar when we apply the line-recovery argument to the inverse map.
Lemma 4.1.
Let F have characteristic p, with F=Fp. If multiplication by r∈Fp×​ on VF​ maps every projective line over Fp into a projective line, then r=1.
Proof.
Represent r by an integer 1≤r<p and take x∈F∖Fp. The points [1],[x],[x+1] lie on one line. Their images under multiplication by r are [1],[xr],[(x+1)r]. The first two are distinct, so the asserted line containment implies
(x+1)r∈Fp+Fpxr.
If 1<r<p, the binomial expansion has nonzero coefficient r at xr−1. This contradicts the linear independence of 1,x,…,xp−1 over Fp from Lemma 2.2.
∎
Proposition 4.2.
Let K/k and L/l be finitely generated extensions of algebraically closed fields of characteristic p, both of transcendence degree at least two. For every compatible isomorphism Θ:VK​→VL​, there is a unique n∈Fp×​ such that Ψ=nΘ sends every projective line over Kp onto a projective line over Lp.
Proof.
Put H=Kp and C=Lp. We first find one scalar for which lines map into lines. Only after this construction will we apply it to the inverse.
A connected graph of independent image pairs. On the nonzero elements of VK​, join [x] and [y] by an edge when
C(X)=C(Y),[X]=Θ([x]),[Y]=Θ([y]).
This condition is independent of the chosen representatives. Since X,Y∈/C, the fields C(X) and C(Y) have degree p over C. An edge therefore means that X,Y are p-independent. The graph is complete between distinct parts of the partition by the fields C(X). It has at least two parts: by Lemma 2.1, [L:C]≥p2, so for any X∈/C there is an element of L∖C(X), and Θ is surjective. Thus every vertex has a neighbor, and any two vertices are joined by a path of length at most two.
An affine configuration along an edge. Fix an edge [x],[y]. The elements 1,x,y are linearly independent over H. Indeed, a dependence would give y=c+dx with c,d∈H and d=0, since x,y∈/H. If c=0, the two vertices would coincide. Otherwise Lemma 2.4 gives {x,y}K​=0, and compatibility followed by Lemma 2.3 gives Y∈C(X), again contradicting the edge condition.
For arbitrary a,b∈H×, set
u=x+a,v=y+b,z=bx−ay=bu−av.(4.1)
These are nonzero: u,v are nonzero because x,y∈/H, and z=0 because x,y are H-linearly independent. Moreover,
[u]∈/Fp​[x],[v]∈/Fp​[y].(4.2)
For example, [u]=i[x] with 0≤i<p would give x+a=hxi for some h∈H×, contrary to the linear independence of 1,x,…,xp−1 and the condition a=0. Figure 1 shows the incidence that explains the two expressions for z.
Lemma 2.4, applied also to z/x=b−a(y/x) and z/u=b−a(v/u), gives
{x,u}K​={y,v}K​={y/x,z/x}K​={v/u,z/u}K​=0.(4.3)
Write [U]=Θ([u]), [V]=Θ([v]), and [Z]=Θ([z]). Compatibility and Lemma 2.3 applied to the first two symbols show that
U∈C(X)×,V∈C(Y)×.
Linearity and injectivity transport (4.2) to [U]∈/Fp​[X] and [V]∈/Fp​[Y]. In particular U,V∈/C. Also Y/X∈/C, since X,Y are p-independent, and V/U∈/C: otherwise U would belong to C(X)∩C(Y)=C. We may therefore apply Lemma 2.3 to the last two symbols in (4.3). The result is
Z∈XC(Y/X)×∩UC(V/U)×.
All hypotheses of Proposition 3.1 now hold. It gives a common integer 1≤n<p such that
Un∈C+CXn,Vn∈C+CYn,(4.4)
and either inclusion uniquely determines n.
Propagation of the scalar. Fix representatives for all vertices and their images. For a vertex [x], fix one neighbor [y] and one b∈H×. As a∈H× varies, Proposition 3.1 applies to (4.1). The second inclusion in (4.4), whose pair Y,V stays fixed, forces the same n for every a. To compare choices of neighbor and b, specialize to a=1, keeping X and a representative U of Θ([x+1]) fixed. Uniqueness for the first inclusion shows that these choices cannot change n. Thus each vertex has a well-defined scalar. Adjacent vertices have the same scalar by (4.4). Connectedness consequently supplies a single n for all vertices and all a∈H×.
Set Ψ=nΘ, with n viewed in Fp×​. The line joining [1] and [x] consists of those two points and [x+a] for a∈H×. The first inclusion in (4.4) says exactly that its image is contained in the line joining [1] and [Xn]. Every projective line is a multiplicative translate of one through [1]: multiply the line joining [s],[t] by s−1. Multiplication by a nonzero field element is linear over the field of p-th powers, and Ψ respects the multiplicative group law. Thus Ψ maps every line into a line.
Equality of lines and uniqueness. Scalar multiplication preserves compatibility, since it scales the tensor square by the nonzero scalar n2. Hence Ψ−1 is compatible. Apply the construction just completed, with the fields reversed, to obtain r∈Fp×​ for which rΨ−1 maps lines into lines. Its composition with Ψ is multiplication by r on VK​ and has the same line-containment property. Lemma 4.1 forces r=1. Thus both Ψ and its inverse map lines into lines. If Ψ(ℓ)⊆ℓ′, choose a line ℓ′′ containing Ψ−1(ℓ′). Then
ℓ⊆Ψ−1(ℓ′)⊆ℓ′′.
Two projective lines cannot properly contain one another, so ℓ=ℓ′′ and both inclusions are equalities. Applying Ψ gives Ψ(ℓ)=ℓ′.
Finally, if mΘ also sends lines onto lines, then (mΘ)∘Ψ−1 is multiplication by mn−1 on VL​ and preserves lines. Another application of Lemma 4.1 gives m=n.
∎

5 From projective lines to the field

Proposition 4.2 has recovered a bijection of projective spaces that preserves both lines and the multiplicative group law. The fundamental theorem of projective geometry [Hall, 2015, Section~8.2, Theorem~8.2] recovers addition from the lines; the group law then forces the resulting additive map to be multiplicative. This last passage also appears in Cadoret and Pirutka (2021), Section~4, Lemma~29. We include the coordinate argument to make both the reconstruction and its uniqueness explicit.
Proposition 5.1 (Projective lifting).
Let E and E′ be finite-dimensional vector spaces over fields H and C, respectively, with dimensions at least three. Every bijection ψ:PH​(E)→PC​(E′) that maps lines onto lines is induced by an additive bijection S:E→E′ satisfying
S(av)=σ(a)S(v)(a∈H, v∈E)
for a field isomorphism σ:H→C. The map σ is unique, and S is unique up to multiplication by an element of C×.
Proof.
The inverse also maps lines onto lines: a target line is the image of the line joining the preimages of any two distinct points on it. Projective spans are obtained by repeatedly joining pairs of points by lines, so ψ and its inverse preserve spans. Minimal spanning sets therefore correspond, and dimH​E=dimC​E′=N+1 for some N≥2. Choose a basis e0​,…,eN​ of E and representatives e0′​,…,eN′​ of their images. They form a basis of E′. Keeping e0′​ fixed, scale each ei′​, i≥1, so that
ψ([e0​+ei​])=[e0′​+ei′​].
This is possible because [e0​+ei​] lies on the line joining [e0​] to [ei​] and differs from both endpoints.
The hyperplanes spanned by e1​,…,eN​ and by e1′​,…,eN′​ correspond. On their affine complements use the coordinates
(t1​,…,tN​)⟷[e0​+t1​e1​+⋯+tN​eN​].
The induced affine bijection preserves parallelism: parallel lines have the same point on the corresponding hyperplane at infinity. On the ith coordinate axis it is a bijection σi​:H→C fixing 0 and 1. Varying only the jth input coordinate moves along a line with point at infinity [ej​], whose image has point at infinity [ej′​]. Hence all other output coordinates are unchanged. It follows that the affine map is
(t1​,…,tN​)⟼(σ1​(t1​),…,σN​(tN​)).
In each plane of two coordinate axes, the diagonal through (0,0) and (1,1) maps to the corresponding diagonal. Thus all σi​ equal one bijection σ:H→C. In the first two coordinates, the line (t,t+a) is parallel to this diagonal and passes through (0,a). Its image therefore gives
σ(t+a)=σ(t)+σ(a).
The line (t,at) passes through (0,0) and (1,a), so its image gives
σ(at)=σ(a)σ(t).
Since σ(1)=1, it is a field isomorphism.
Define S(∑i=0N​ti​ei​)=∑i=0N​σ(ti​)ei′​. This is an additive, σ-semilinear bijection inducing ψ on the affine chart. Every point at infinity is the direction of an affine line through the origin, so it induces ψ there as well.
For uniqueness, suppose that T is another semilinear lift, possibly with a different field isomorphism. For every nonzero v∈E write T(v)=cv​S(v) with cv​∈C×. If v,w are independent, additivity applied to v+w and independence of S(v),S(w) give cv​=cw​=cv+w​. Two dependent nonzero vectors can each be compared to a vector outside their common line. Thus cv​ is a single scalar c, and T=cS. Comparing the images of av then shows that the two field isomorphisms also agree.
∎
We will also recover the prescribed algebraically closed base directly from the field.
Lemma 5.2.
If F/κ is a finitely generated extension of an algebraically closed field of characteristic p, then
m≥1⋂​Fpm=κ.
Proof.
Perfectness gives the inclusion from right to left. If f∈F∖κ, algebraic closedness makes f transcendental over κ. Complete f to a transcendence basis f,t2​,…,td​, and put B=κ(t2​,…,td​) and E=B(f). The extension F/E is finite; write D=[F:E]. For every m≥1, the polynomial Tpm−f is Eisenstein at the prime f of B[f], and is therefore irreducible over E. If f=gpm with g∈F, it follows that
pm=[E(g):E]≤D.
This fails for all sufficiently large m, so f does not belong to the intersection.
∎
Proof of Theorem 1.1.
A field isomorphism α:K→L sends Kp to Lp and Steinberg pairs to Steinberg pairs. It therefore induces an element of IsomM​(VK​,VL​), and the canonical map in the theorem is well defined.
For surjectivity, take Θ∈IsomM​(VK​,VL​). Proposition 4.2 gives n∈Fp×​ such that Ψ=nΘ maps lines onto lines. Put H=Kp and C=Lp. By Lemma 2.1, dimH​K and dimC​L are at least p2≥4, so Proposition 5.1 gives a semilinear lift S:K→L. Since Ψ([1])=[1], scale S to arrange S(1)=1. For each f∈K×, the two semilinear bijections
w⟼S(fw),w⟼S(f)S(w)
induce the same projective map: the equality is precisely Ψ([fw])=Ψ([f])+Ψ([w]) in the additive notation for VL​. Their values at 1 agree, so the uniqueness assertion in Proposition 5.1 makes them equal. Thus S is multiplicative, and hence a field isomorphism. It maps every Kpm onto Lpm, so Lemma 5.2 gives S(k)=l. Its induced map is nΘ, proving surjectivity onto the scalar quotient.
For injectivity, suppose that field isomorphisms α,β:K→L induce maps with β∗​=rα∗​ for r∈Fp×​. Both preserve projective lines, so multiplication by r on VL​ also preserves lines. Lemma 4.1 gives r=1. The maps α and β are therefore semilinear lifts of the same projective bijection. Proposition 5.1 makes them scalar multiples, and α(1)=β(1)=1 makes them equal.
∎
Remark 5.3 (Frobenius and the target quotient).
There is no further Frobenius ambiguity. For a field F/κ as in the theorem, the Frobenius map F→F, f↦fp, is not surjective and induces the zero map on VF​. By contrast, F→Fp is a field isomorphism, whose induced isomorphism has target
VFp​=(Fp)×/(Fp2)×.
It is already covered by the theorem, with its actual target field Fp.
